15.0.s.en: (1) Absalom wins the people to his side

15.0.0.en: After Absalom had won the favor of his father King David, he began to carry out his plans to seize the kingdom from him. He surrounded himself with displays of grandeur and went about in a procession in a chariot, like a prince and crown prince, with horsemen on horses before him and runners running ahead to clear the way for him, announcing his passing through the place. He had learned this from his pagan grandfather, his mother's father, the king of Geshur. David, however, was humble and rode on a mule, as God had commanded in the Law. Absalom ran after displays of grandeur, while David endured many afflictions, and in the end reigned over his people and remained humble.

15.1.0.en: Absalom would go early in the morning to the gate of the city, where the judges held their sessions to judge the people's cases. He would meet those who had cases and would flatter them, pretending to appreciate their problems and trying to draw close to them and get to know them by asking which tribe they belonged to, and they would answer his questions, glad of his interest in them. When he heard the problem of one of them, he would assure him that the right was on his side and that he was not in the wrong in anything, and he would say the same thing to his opponent if he also came. Then he would cast doubt on the justice of the judges whom the king appointed, accusing them of injustice, partiality and corruption in judgment, and so he led them to hate the king and weakened their trust in him.

15.2.0.en: Absalom claimed before them that if he sat on the seat of judgment, he would do justice to every man who had a suit.

15.3.0.en: He dealt with those who came for judgment in a manner that made them feel his humility as well as his sympathy with their problems. If any of them tried to bow down to him out of respect for his position as a prince, he would not let him bow down, but would raise him up, draw him near, and kiss him.

15.4.0.en: They come for judgment: they appear before the judges to have their cases heard.

15.4.1.en: He stole the hearts of the men of Israel: he won their hearts to himself, and they loved him.

15.4.2.en: Such was his conduct toward everyone who came for judgment from all the tribes of Israel, and by it he drew their hearts to himself and they loved him.

15.4.3.en: Do not be a hypocrite and deceive others, showing affection and love in order to achieve your own purposes. Rather, be sincere in showing good feelings, so that you may reveal to them the Christ who dwells in you and win them to Him.

15.5.s.en: (2) Absalom plots a coup against his father King David

15.5.0.en: Forty years after Samuel anointed David king, Absalom began to take an actual step to seize the kingdom. He claimed to his father that he had a vow to the Lord that he must fulfill, and asked him to allow him to go to Hebron to worship the Lord and offer sacrifices. This was merely an outward pretense; in truth he was preparing to stir up a rebellion against his father starting from Hebron, organizing his movement there, far from his father. The people of Hebron were the first over whom David had reigned when he reigned over the tribe of Judah only (2 Sam 5:5) after the death of Saul, and they were distressed by David's later move to Jerusalem, which belonged to the tribe of Benjamin. In addition, Absalom had been born there and had lived the beginning of his life there, so he must have had friends there and relationships with them.

15.6.0.en: David did not object to allowing his son to go to Hebron to worship and offer sacrifices. On the contrary, he was glad of it, because it meant that his son was drawing near to God, and he blessed him with a prayer for his safety, and Absalom set out for Hebron.

15.7.0.en: From Hebron Absalom sent his men throughout the land and gave them instructions that when they heard the sound of the trumpets, they were to spread among the tribes that this meant that Absalom was reigning in Hebron, so that they would make the whole people believe that Absalom had officially become king over the land.

15.8.0.en: To complete his plan of seizing power without any right, he invited two hundred of the notables of the people to a feast he held in Hebron, and they accepted his invitation in good faith, not knowing that by this he wanted to make the people believe that he was supported as king by the leaders of the people. He also wanted to keep them away from Jerusalem so that they would not help the king against him, and likewise to weaken his father's morale, as he would feel that the leaders had left him and become supporters of Absalom. Besides, he was preparing the plan to convince them to accept him as king in place of his father.

15.8.1.en: Beware of pride, for it drags its owners into many troubles and makes them like the blind, so that they fall into various sins. Guard against it by submitting to your spiritual father, learning from those around you, and attending to your repentance every day, so that you live in humility.

15.9.s.en: (3) David learns of Absalom's rebellion and leaves Jerusalem

15.9.0.en: Giloh: a village in the hills of Judah, about 8 km northwest of Hebron.

15.9.1.en: Absalom sent for a wise man named Ahithophel, summoning him from his town "Giloh," where he was at that time offering sacrifices. This Ahithophel was originally a counselor to David, but sadly he betrayed his lord David and joined Absalom. Confusion spread through the land: some welcomed Absalom as king and some held fast to David as king, because Absalom's affability toward the people had led many to accept him, in addition to the organized propaganda for him in all the tribes.

15.9.2.en: In their betrayal of David, Absalom and Ahithophel are a type of Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Christ and sold Him.

15.10.0.en: The news of Absalom's rebellion reached David from his loyal men, and that he had declared himself king and many had rallied around him.

15.11.0.en: David understood, by his experience and the wisdom God had given him, that the situation was serious, so he ordered his men to leave the city of Jerusalem, lest Absalom destroy it and kill them and everyone in Jerusalem. Perhaps he remembered at that time God's punishment of him after his fall into adultery and murder, that the sword would never depart from his house, and so he accepted what Absalom did with humility and submission to God.

15.12.0.en: All submitted to the king's command and showed their complete readiness to carry out everything he commanded them, for they were his loyal men.

15.13.0.en: Concubines: female servants with whom the king had lived.

15.13.1.en: The king left his palace in Jerusalem, fleeing outside the city with his wives and his sons, and left ten of his concubines in the house in an attempt to preserve the royal palace if possible.

15.14.0.en: All David's men and his household followed him out of Jerusalem, and they gathered at the last house in the city to cross from there to the outside of the city. During this, David said the third Psalm: "LORD, how are they increased that trouble me!" "... he that did eat of my bread (Ahithophel) hath lifted up his heel against me."

15.15.0.en: The Pelethites: they are the police and the royal guard in the present day.

15.15.1.en: The Cherethites: the infantry of the army.

15.15.2.en: The Gittites: the people of the city of Gath, one of the five great Philistine cities.

15.15.3.en: David stood at the gate of the city, and his men began to cross to the outside of it before him one by one, and with them the police, the infantry of the army, the soldiers, and the Gittites who had accompanied David during his periods of flight from Saul, had converted to Judaism, and had become loyal to David; the number of the Gittites was 600 men.

15.15.4.en: It is good to be realistic, to meet adverse situations with wisdom, and to act quickly so that no harm comes to you. Lift your heart in prayer to God and He will guide you; do not yield to illusions and wishful thinking, but ask for God's help, and you will bear the affliction and pass through it until it ends.

15.16.s.en: (4) Ittai the Gittite insists on accompanying David

15.16.0.en: Ittai the Gittite: a man from the city of "Gath," who was the commander of the six hundred Gittite men mentioned above.

15.16.1.en: Ittai, a Philistine man from Gath, wanted to go out with David and accompany him in his flight from Jerusalem, but David did not want to burden him with the hardship of the pursuit to which he would be exposed. There was no reason for it, since he was a foreigner and far from his own country, and the matter might not concern him at all; he could stay in Jerusalem to serve the new king, for he had come to the land of Judah only a short time before, and it was not proper for him to wander about with David, for David did not know where matters would settle for him. So he asked him to return to Jerusalem and to take his six hundred Gittite men with him as well. David prayed for him, asking mercy from the Lord for the loyalty he had shown toward him, and asked the Lord to reward him with good.

15.16.2.en: We note that this account is an elaboration of what is mentioned in (v. 18); the historical order is that David told them to go back, and when they insisted on following him, they crossed to the outside of the city with the Pelethites and the Cherethites.

15.17.0.en: Ittai swore by the living God that he would not leave his lord but would stay with him in every circumstance, whether God willed to give him life or death. In his following of David, Ittai is a type of the Gentiles who followed Christ, while Absalom, in his rejection of David his father, is a type of the Jews who crucified Christ.

15.18.0.en: In the face of the determination and resolve that Ittai showed not to abandon his lord, David allowed him to cross with the people going out of Jerusalem, and he crossed, he and his six hundred men and all their little ones and their wives.

15.18.1.en: How great is this loyalty and love from Ittai, a man of foreign race! It is remarkable that David is betrayed by his son, yet is supported by strangers who loved him, just as he was supported before by Jonathan and Michal, the children of Saul, who was persecuting him. May you be loyal to every person who has shown you love, and above all be loyal to God, so that you do not betray Him by committing sin, and if you sin, return to Him quickly in repentance.

15.19.s.en: (5) The Ark of God is sent back from the field of battle

15.19.0.en: The Kidron Valley: its present name is the Valley of Sitt Maryam, and it is sometimes called the Valley of Jehoshaphat; it extends from the northwest of Jerusalem to its southeast.

15.19.1.en: The way of the wilderness: the wilderness of the Jordan between Jerusalem and Jericho.

15.19.2.en: Sorrow filled all of Jerusalem, and the people were weeping over what had befallen. The king went out with his men and they came to the Kidron Valley, and all the people went out with him and passed through the wilderness of the Jordan (between Jerusalem and Jericho). And as David crossed this valley, so also Christ crossed this valley on His way to the garden of Gethsemane on the night of His sufferings (Jn 18:1).

15.20.0.en: Zadok: of the descendants of Eleazar son of Aaron, and one of the two great priests in the days of David; he remained faithful to him during Adonijah's attempt to seize the kingdom.

15.20.1.en: Out of the priests' love for David and their feeling that he was the true king, Zadok and Abiathar brought out the Ark and set it down at the gate of the city, so that all the people going out of the city might pass before it, to lift their morale and give them the feeling that God was in their midst and was their helper.

15.21.0.en: David preferred that the Ark remain in Jerusalem, so he asked Zadok to return it to its place, for if the Lord willed to bring David back to his kingdom, He would let him see the Ark and the tabernacle of meeting again, and if the Lord was not pleased with him, let Him do to him as seems good in His eyes. This shows how great David's concern was for the Ark: it should remain in its place and not be taken out as the sons of Eli the priest took it out in their war with the Philistines, and they were defeated and the Philistines took the Ark (1 Sam 4, 5). The Ark must stay firmly in its place, while David was merely a man: either God would be pleased with him and bring him back to his kingdom, or He would not bring him back because he did not deserve it. This was great humility on David's part.

15.21.1.en: This is a lesson for us from our teacher David: that we should always surrender our lives to the Lord so that He may accomplish His will in them according to His good pleasure, and accept with thanksgiving everything the Lord allows for us.

15.22.0.en: You are a seer: full of wisdom and understanding, able to judge matters and see which is right. Abiathar: the other great priest, who conspired with Adonijah to take the kingdom for him.

15.22.1.en: Ahimaaz son of Zadok and Jonathan son of Abiathar: they remained in Jerusalem during Absalom's rebellion and used to inform David of Absalom's plans, and Ahimaaz was the first to tell David of Absalom's defeat. David asked Zadok to return to Jerusalem, together with Ahimaaz his son and Jonathan son of Abiathar, so that he might follow the course of events inside the city, analyze them with his wisdom, and send David a report on the situation.

15.23.0.en: David made the two great priests Zadok and Abiathar understand that he would slow his pace in the plains of the wilderness of the Jordan, waiting for them to bring him word of the movements of Absalom and his men around the city after watching them closely, and to send him news of all the details by their two sons.

15.24.0.en: Zadok and Abiathar carried out David's directions, and they carried the Ark back to its place in Jerusalem and stayed there watching for Absalom's movements, so as to inform David of everything that happened.

15.24.1.en: (6) Ahithophel joins Absalom, and David seeks the help of Hushai the Archite to defeat Ahithophel's counsel (vv. 30-37:) 30And David went up by the ascent of mount Olivet, and wept as he went up, and had his head covered, and he went barefoot: and all the people that was with him covered every man his head, and they went up, weeping as they went up. 31And one told David, saying, Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom. And David said, "O LORD, I pray thee, turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness." 32And it came to pass, that when David was come to the top of the mount, where he worshipped God, behold, Hushai the Archite came to meet him with his coat rent, and earth upon his head: 33Unto whom David said, "If thou passest on with me, then thou shalt be a burden unto me: 34But if thou return to the city, and say unto Absalom, I will be thy servant, O king; as I have been thy father's servant hitherto, so will I now also be thy servant: then mayest thou for me defeat the counsel of Ahithophel. 35And hast thou not there with thee Zadok and Abiathar the priests? therefore it shall be, that what thing soever thou shalt hear out of the king's house, thou shalt tell it to Zadok and Abiathar the priests. 36Behold, they have there with them their two sons, Ahimaaz Zadok's son, and Jonathan Abiathar's son; and by them ye shall send unto me every thing that ye can hear." 37So Hushai David's friend came into the city, and Absalom came into Jerusalem.

15.25.0.en: The Mount of Olives: east of the Kidron Valley, which separates it from Jerusalem.

15.25.1.en: David and his men went up the Mount of Olives, and the scene was deeply moving: David was weeping with his head covered as a sign of intense grief, and walking barefoot as a sign of abasement, and all the people accompanying him did likewise. David had not wept before during Saul's pursuit of him, but here he weeps because the betrayal came from his son, and perhaps he remembered at that time his sins of adultery and murder, so he wept in repentance, humbling himself before God.

15.26.0.en: Turn into foolishness: make his counsel wrong, vain and useless.

15.26.1.en: David learned that his former counselor Ahithophel had joined Absalom's camp, so he prayed to the Lord to bring to nothing the counsel of Ahithophel that he might give to Absalom (Ps 41:11). David's goodness is shown in that he did not ask for harm to come to Ahithophel the traitor, but only for his counsel to be brought to nothing.

15.27.0.en: David reached the top of the Mount of Olives and worshipped there. Hushai the Archite, one of David's counselors, had been absent from Jerusalem during that period, and when he learned of the events he went at once to David with his clothes torn and earth on his head, as a sign of intense grief, wishing to accompany his lord wherever he went.

15.28.0.en: David saw that Hushai's going out with him would add nothing to the strength of his army but would increase his burdens, because he would have to provide for his needs, and Hushai was not a man of war, being a man of counsel, and it was more profitable for David to benefit from his abilities. So he asked him to return to Jerusalem and pretend to serve Absalom as he had served his father, and to give counsel that opposed the counsel of Ahithophel, and this is what in fact happened, as we shall see later. And David repeated Psalm 41: "Mine enemies speak evil of me."

15.28.1.en: God always sends help to His servants in due time, so we should pray to Him, asking for help in distress, and He is able to use whomever He wills to bring us deliverance from dangers.

15.29.0.en: David assigned him a useful task and informed him that he would find in Jerusalem both Zadok and Abiathar with their two sons, and that Hushai was to watch everything that happened around Absalom and what was said in his council in conversations with his followers, and to report all that he saw and heard to the two priests, who would send it with their two sons to David. All this arrangement was for David's protection and involved no wrong to Absalom, but was an attempt to stop his evil. It will appear later how great was David's love and concern for the life of his son Absalom despite all the evil he had done against him.

15.30.0.en: Hushai carried out David's request and returned to the city of Jerusalem, and the time of his arrival coincided with the arrival of Absalom, who entered it to take possession of it and set himself up as king over Israel. The meeting of Ziba and Shimei with David, and Absalom's entry into Jerusalem
